source: Chen et al. (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: The founding self-debugging loop: sample a program, run it, show the model the result, let it fix. The model also explains its own code line by line (rubber-duck style) before fixing. Feedback comes in four kinds: simple (right/wrong), unit-test output (UT), code explanation (Expl), and execution trace.
numbers: Paper reports gains up to 12% (TransCoder, MBPP with unit tests) and 2-3% on Spider (no tests). Models: Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, StarCoder.
quote: Self-Debugging with code explanation consistently improves the baseline by 2 - 3%
limits: Few-shot prompts for Codex; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 did not follow exemplars as well. Gains are mostly on tasks where the first try is close to right.
agent_relevance: This is the base loop for S4 TEST and S5 REVISE: test, show real output, revise. It matches G2.

source: Chen et al. (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Richer feedback beat simple pass/fail feedback when real execution output was in it. On TransCoder, unit-test plus explanation was best for Codex and GPT-4. On MBPP, unit-test plus trace was best for Codex.
numbers: TransCoder: Codex 80.4 baseline, 89.3 simple, 92.5 UT+Expl. GPT-4 77.3 baseline, 80.9 simple, 90.4 UT+Expl (+13.1). MBPP: Codex 61.4 baseline, 68.2 simple, 70.8 UT+Trace. GPT-4 72.8 baseline, 78.8 simple, 80.6 UT. StarCoder MBPP 47.2 to 53.2 with trace.
limits: Table text was read from a PDF extraction where columns are misaligned; row labels were matched by pattern. Extra gain from explanation over plain unit-test feedback is small (0 to 2 points) on MBPP.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain is from executing the program and showing the real failing output. Explanation adds little on top. Keep S4 output as the main signal.

source: Chen et al. (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Without any execution, self-debugging gains shrink a lot. Strong chat models were overconfident in their first answer and rarely changed it.
numbers: No-execution runs: Codex gains up to 5%. GPT-4 gains 3.6% on MBPP and about 1% on other tasks. GPT-3.5 on TransCoder stays at 89.1 in every no-test condition (baseline 89.1).
limits: Few-shot exemplars did not help GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 here, so they relied on internal knowledge.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: revision needs a real signal. Without a check, a revise step gives little or nothing.

source: Chen et al. (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Self-debugging saves samples. One debugging turn on a greedy answer matched 16 plain samples on Spider. Debugging 8 samples beat 32 plain samples. Almost all of the gain comes in the first turn.
numbers: Spider with Codex: extra turns after the first add within 0.1%. Extra-hard SQL queries gain 9%.
limits: Compares sample counts, not tokens. Debug turns cost extra tokens for explanation and feedback, which the paper does not count against the baseline.
agent_relevance: One revision round is the efficient default (G11). A second round needs its own evidence.

source: Chen et al. (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: What got fixed: small mistakes in nearly-right programs, not deep redesign. On Spider the fixes were mostly missing WHERE conditions, DISTINCT and JOIN clauses. On MBPP and TransCoder, 60 to 70% of fixes were output mismatches in code close to correct.
numbers: Spider fixed errors: wrong WHERE 25.7%, missing DISTINCT 17.1%, wrong JOIN 14.3%, wrong SELECT column count 11.4%. Output mismatch share: TransCoder 61.9%, MBPP 69.2%. Runtime errors 38.1% and 30.8%.
limits: Fix categories come from labelling successful cases only. They say nothing about what failed to be fixed.
agent_relevance: Revision is a local-repair operator. For a wrong frame or wrong approach it is the wrong tool; use the impasse path (S6).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside signal) does not help reasoning and often hurts. Gains reported by earlier papers came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0 [CORRECTED by cross-check from Table 2 of the PDF]. Without oracle, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7 over rounds 0 to 2; CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Reasoning tasks (math, commonsense, multi-hop QA), not code with real tests. The feedback prompts are the authors' own and may be weak.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G3. A revise step must be gated by real output. The model cannot judge its own correctness.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: On GSM8K with GPT-3.5, 74.7% of the time the model kept its initial answer after self-correction. Among changed answers, correct-to-incorrect was more common than incorrect-to-correct.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 after two rounds: 74.7% unchanged. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 changed answers much more often, with a high correct-to-incorrect share (exact bar labels are garbled in the extraction, not recorded).
limits: Only the GSM8K 74.7% figure is reliable from the text.
agent_relevance: A self-critique prompt biases the model toward changing answers. This is a concrete cost of unscheduled doubt (G1).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat plain self-consistency at the same number of responses. Reported gains of debate are mostly extra sampling.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: standard 76.7 (1 response); self-consistency 82.5 at 3, 85.3 at 6, 88.2 at 9 responses. Debate at 3 responses is only slightly above self-consistency at 3 and clearly below it at 6 and 9 responses (text statement; table cells garbled).
limits: One model family, one dataset in this table.
agent_relevance: Support for G9 (no debate) and G4. At equal compute, vote in code.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Many reported self-correction gains came from a weak first prompt. If the requirement sits only in the feedback prompt, the gain comes from the extra instructions, not from correction.
numbers: Example: Constrained Generation from Self-Refine; the original first-turn prompt did not say that all 20 to 30 concepts must be used (exact numbers of the fixed-prompt rerun not recorded).
limits: Numbers for the fixed-prompt rerun not recorded here.
agent_relevance: G7: always compare the loop against a plain baseline given the full instruction at equal tokens.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion for code: write the function, write up to 6 self-generated unit tests, run them, write a verbal self-reflection on the failure, keep it in memory, try again. It reported 91% on HumanEval Python versus 80.1% for GPT-4.
numbers: Pass@1: HumanEval Py 80.1 to 91.0; HumanEval Rust 60.0 to 68.0; MBPP Py 80.1 to 77.1 (worse); MBPP Rust 70.9 to 75.4; Leetcode Hard Py 7.5 to 15.0. Tests are self-generated, so pass@1 stays eligible.
limits: GPT-4 in the main table. MBPP Python went down. Single runs per cell reported.
agent_relevance: Verbal self-reflection from real test output can pay when tests are reliable. See the false-positive result next.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion's gain depends on how trustworthy the self-written tests are. On MBPP Python 16.3% of programs that passed the self-made tests were wrong, versus 1.4% on HumanEval Python. That is why MBPP got worse.
numbers: False positive rate (pass tests but wrong): MBPP Py 0.16 vs HumanEval Py 0.01. False negatives: 0.59 MBPP Py, 0.40 HumanEval Py. Base to Reflexion: HumanEval Py 0.80 to 0.91; MBPP Py 0.80 to 0.77.
limits: The tests are written by the same model that wrote the code, so their errors are correlated with the code's errors.
agent_relevance: Direct case for G3 and G4: a pass on tests the same model wrote is weak proof. Use held-out or code-derived checks.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems: removing self-generated tests was worse than baseline, and removing the written reflection gave no gain. Both parts were needed.
numbers: GPT-4 base 0.60; no test generation (reflection only) 0.52; tests but no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68.
limits: Small subset (n=50), one model, Rust compiler gives rich error text. Differences of 0.08 are 4 problems.
agent_relevance: Two pieces matter: a check to decide whether to revise (G2), and an explanation of the failure before the fix. Without the check, the loop made harmful edits and could not stop early.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Self-correction in Reflexion needs a strong model. StarChat-beta showed no gain.
numbers: StarChat-beta HumanEval Python: baseline 0.26 and Reflexion 0.26 (8 trials averaged, std 0.0048 and 0.0031).
limits: One weak model. Authors call self-correction an emergent quality of stronger, larger models.
agent_relevance: A loop design is not model-free. Test the loop on the actual agent model before trusting any published gain (G7).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-Refine: the same model gives feedback on its own output and then refines it, repeated. Gains were large on subjective or easy-to-spec tasks and near zero on math.
numbers: Math Reasoning base to refined: GPT-3.5 64.1 to 64.1; ChatGPT 74.8 to 75.0; GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1. With an oracle stop signal: GPT-3.5 64.06 to 68.9. Code Optimization GPT-4 27.3 to 36.0; Code Readability GPT-4 15.0 to 45.0. Abstract claims about 20% absolute average gain over seven tasks.
limits: Most tasks are judged by a model or a metric the loop can shape. Code tasks here are optimisation and readability, not bug repair.
agent_relevance: Self-critique gives gains only when the critique is specific and has a signal. For correctness of reasoning there is nothing to gain without outside checks (G2).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Specific feedback matters. Replacing specific feedback with generic feedback, or none, cut gains. Sentiment reversal fell from 43.2 to 31.2 (generic) to 0 (no feedback). In code optimisation the spread was only 2.7 points.
numbers: Feedback ablation (score): Code Optimization 27.5 specific, 26.0 generic, 24.8 none. Sentiment Reversal 43.2, 31.2, 0. Acronym Generation 56.4, 54.0, 48.0.
limits: No confidence intervals in this table in the main text; 2.7 points may be noise.
agent_relevance: In code, the gain from model-written feedback is small. Do not count on critique text alone.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair is not a silver bullet. When repair cost is counted in tokens (pass@t), gains over simply drawing more independent samples are often modest, vary by dataset and subset, and sometimes do not exist.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS; Code Llama 13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. np up to 25 samples, 1 feedback and 1 repair per failure. On APPS only GPT-4 benefits significantly; Code Llama and GPT-3.5 match or trail their no-repair baselines. At small budgets the gain is marginal or absent.
quote: self-repair is not a silver bullet for code generation
limits: Models are weaker than 2025 models; unit-test feedback only; one-shot repair, not an agent.
agent_relevance: Strongest equal-compute evidence against a plain revise loop. G7 and G12: check a revise loop against resampling at the same tokens.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: The bottleneck of self-repair is the model's feedback about its own code. Swapping in a stronger model for the feedback step gave large gains. Expert human feedback raised the repair success rate of GPT-4 by 1.58 times.
numbers: Repair success, GPT-4 own feedback vs human feedback: overall 33.30% vs 52.60%; introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%. Code Llama and GPT-3.5 with a stronger feedback model beat both their baselines and their own self-repair on APPS.
limits: Human study is small; human time cost not measured. The stronger-feedback arm uses a bigger model, so it is not an equal-compute test.
agent_relevance: Localising and explaining the fault is the hard step, not writing the patch. Spend effort on the diagnosis slot (O5) and feed it real runtime facts (G2).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Repair and resampling success trend together by difficulty. Stronger models fix easy tasks more often but also solve them from scratch more often, so the net benefit of repair is hard to predict. Diversity of the initial programs matters.
numbers: Paper conclusion: gains rely on sufficient diversity in the initial programs. Per-difficulty success rates are in Appendix C figures (not recorded).
limits: Qualitative reading of trend figures.
agent_relevance: Gate revision by difficulty and by prior success (G12): repair only where the first attempt is close.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB
finding: LDB: instead of only pass/fail, split the program into basic blocks, record actual variable values at each block from a real run, and ask the model to say for each block whether it is right. A breakpoint-style debugging loop.
numbers: Gains up to 9.8% over baseline on HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. HumanEval GPT-3.5 seed 73.8 to 82.9 (LDB, +9.1) vs Self-Debug 81.1 (+7.3). GPT-4 seeds 87.2 to 89.6 (LDB) vs 88.4 (SD). Reflexion seeds 91.5 to 95.1 (LDB) vs 92.1 (SD). Debugger is GPT-3.5. Time per problem 17.23 s (LDB) vs 17.08 s (SD).
limits: Comparison inside the authors' own paper, one run. Differences of 1.7 to 3 points on 164 problems are 3 to 5 problems.
agent_relevance: Real runtime values beat model-simulated traces. Supports G2: locate from actual output with code. Our O5 should supply real variable values, not ask the model to guess them.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB
finding: Self-Debug's model-simulated trace can mislead. The LDB authors say the model cannot compute concrete values or branches reliably, so a wrong trace sends repair the wrong way. They link this to Self-Debug giving no gain with StarCoder on HumanEval.
numbers: StarCoder HumanEval (baseline 39.0): SD (+Expl.) 38.4 (-0.6), SD (+Trace) 39.0 (+0.0), LDB 39.6 (+0.6). Granularity, GPT-3.5: block-level 82.9 (6.2 turns), line-level 80.5 (6.4), function-level 79.9 (8.1). CodeLlama: 55.5 block, 53.7 line, 53.7 function from 49.4.
limits: The mechanism is the authors' explanation, not isolated by an experiment. CodeLlama gains are small.
agent_relevance: Granularity is tunable: block-sized units beat both lines and whole functions. Use a middle chunk size in S4/S5.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB
finding: At more debugging rounds LDB kept improving up to 10 iterations, while repeated sampling and Self-Debug flattened earlier.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-3.5: LDB about 84.1 at iteration 10; Self-Debug about 81 to 82; repeated sampling about 80 to 81 (values read from a garbled figure).
limits: Equal rounds, not equal tokens. Figure values read approximately.
agent_relevance: Extra rounds help only when each round adds new real information.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: AutoFL: the model navigates a repository by calling functions (get class, get method code, get comments) to find the faulty method and explain the bug. It beats spectrum-based fault localisation (Ochiai) on method-level acc@1 with less information, but with GPT-3.5 it lags SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5.
numbers: 798 bugs, Defects4J and BugsInPy. Method-level acc@1 gain over Ochiai: +19.7% (Defects4J, GPT-3.5), +166.7% (BugsInPy, GPT-3.5), +233.3% (BugsInPy, GPT-4). Five runs per bug.
limits: Gains are relative percentages on small base numbers. Data leakage of famous bugs possible; checked only by a no-tools GPT-3.5 baseline that did worse.
agent_relevance: Fault localisation by a tool-using LLM is competitive. Pairs with O5 and G2: code gives the failing test and call information, the model picks the location.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: Repeating the localiser gives a usable confidence signal. Agreement across runs correlates with correctness, but only about 1 in 5 explanations is right about the root cause.
numbers: Spearman correlation of confidence with Precision@1: 0.57 (Defects4J) and 0.52 (BugsInPy). 300 explanations from 60 bugs: 20% accurate about the root cause; 26.3% had at least one inaccurate statement; 56.7% of bugs had at least one accurate explanation in 5 runs; 83.7% of runs finished within token and call budget. Inter-rater agreement 0.55.
limits: Small manual sample, two raters, kappa 0.55. Confidence comes from samples of the same model, so errors are correlated (G4).
agent_relevance: Agreement is a hint (G4). Use it to decide when to spend more, not as proof of the root cause.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: SWE-agent shows the interface matters as much as the model. A tool layer designed for the LM (100-line file viewer, compact search, edit command with built-in linter) beat a plain shell by 64% relative with the same GPT-4 Turbo.
numbers: SWE-bench 2,294 tasks: SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo 12.47% (286), Claude 3 Opus 10.46%. SWE-bench Lite (300): 18.00% (54) vs Shell-only 11.00% vs RAG 2.67% (GPT-4 Turbo). Lite cost per task: SWE-agent about $1.67 vs RAG $0.13. HumanEvalFix pass@1 88.3%.
limits: Single run per setting for most rows; per-instance variance is large. SWE-agent costs 8 to 13x RAG.
agent_relevance: The scaffold's tools carry much of the gain, so tool design counts toward G7 setup cost. Real feedback in the loop (G2).

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Ablations of SWE-agent on SWE-bench Lite: the linter guardrail on edits adds 3 points, having no edit tool costs 7.7 points, a 100-line viewer window beats 30 lines or the whole file, and iterative search is worse than no search.
numbers: Edit: no edit tool 10.3; edit action 15.0; edit with linting 18.0. Search: summarised 18.0; none 15.7; iterative 12.0. Viewer: 30 lines 14.3; 100 lines 18.0; full file 12.7. Context: last 5 observations 18.0; full history 15.0; no demonstration 16.3.
limits: Each ablation is one run on 300 tasks (one task is 0.33 points), so differences of 1 to 3 points are inside run noise.
agent_relevance: Guardrails against bad edits help, context must be trimmed, and too much or too little shown at once lowers success. Matches G11 and G7.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Failure modes in SWE-agent trajectories: repeated bad edits, cascading failed edits, and wrong implementations. Recovery odds fall fast after a failed edit, and failed runs run longer and cost more than solved ones.
numbers: 1,185 of 2,294 trajectories (51.7%) had 1 or more failed edits. Chance an edit attempt eventually works: 90.5%; after one failed edit: 57.2%. Unresolved Lite runs (n=248, labelled by GPT-4o, 87% agreement with authors): incorrect or overly specific implementation 52.0%, cascading failed edits 23.4%. Solved: median 12 steps and $1.21; unsolved mean 21 steps and $2.52. 93.0% of solved runs finish before the cost cap.
limits: Failure labels are LLM-assigned. Median vs mean comparison mixes statistics. 'Succeed fast, fail slow' is correlation: easy tasks finish early.
agent_relevance: Strong support for an impasse detector (S6): after 2 failed edits the loop should stop revising the same snippet and change approach. More budget is unlikely to help (G12).

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: Agentless: no agent. Three fixed phases: localise (files, classes, functions, lines), repair (sample many candidate patches), and validate (generate reproduction tests, run them with regression tests, vote). It beat open-source agents at lower cost on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite GPT-4o: 32.00% (96/300) at $0.70 per issue. For comparison in its Table 1: SWE-agent GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62; SWE-agent Claude 3.5 Sonnet 23.00%; AutoCodeRover GPT-4o 21.67%; AutoCodeRover-v2 30.67%; Aider 26.33% at $1.14; OpenDevin CodeAct 26.67%.
limits: Closed-source commercial tools were competitive at the time. A fixed pipeline cannot adapt mid-run. Lite problems are easier than full SWE-bench.
agent_relevance: A code-driven pipeline with sampled attempts and a code-run selector wins at lower cost. This is our stance: the program decides, the model fills slots.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: The selection step is where Agentless gets its gain. Majority vote over the candidate patches gave 77 fixes; adding regression tests gave 81; adding model-written reproduction tests gave 96.
numbers: Patch selection ablation: majority voting 77 (25.67%) $0.00; +regression test 81 (27.00%) $0.01; +reproduction test 96 (32.00%) $0.25. A reproduction test is kept only if it prints the issue-reproduced message on the original repo.
limits: Reproduction tests are model-written and can be wrong; when none pass, Agentless falls back to regression tests only.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G3 and G5: code runs selection. A test that fails before and passes after is a real check on the failure itself.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: SWE-bench Lite has flawed items. A hand analysis of all 300 found exact patches in the issue text, missing information, and misleading suggested fixes.
numbers: 4.3% of Lite problems contain the exact ground-truth patch in the description; a further 9.7% describe the exact steps; 10.0% miss critical information; 5.0% contain misleading proposed solutions. The filtered set SWE-bench Lite-S has 249 problems.
limits: Manual labelling by the authors; the filter is one group's judgement.
agent_relevance: Benchmark gains on Lite overstate real debugging ability. Prefer our own hold-out checks (G3).

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement
finding: AutoCodeRover: the model searches the code with structure-aware tools (find class, method, snippet) in layers, then writes a patch. Optional spectrum-based fault localisation (SBFL) from tests gives hints and lifts results.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: ACR @1 19.00% (57) at $0.43 and 195 s; ACR @3 26.00% (78) at $1.30; ACR with SBFL 22.00% (66). Full SWE-bench 12.42% @1, 17.96% @3. SWE-agent on Lite 18.00% at $2.51. Unique solves: ACR 26, SWE-agent 23.
limits: @3 means any of three runs solved it, so it is not comparable to pass@1. GPT-4 (0125). Single run each.
agent_relevance: Program-derived fault localisation (SBFL, +3 points) complements LLM search. It fits O5: locate backwards from the failing test with code, not opinion.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
finding: SWE-bench: 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories. The task is to edit the repo so the failing tests pass. At release, models did poorly even with a perfect file retriever.
numbers: Abstract: Claude 2 solves 4.8% and GPT-4 1.7% of instances with an oracle retriever. The reference fix typically edits about 15 lines in one function, in repos of up to 1,900 files and 400K lines. Pass-to-pass tests guard against regressions.
limits: Only the abstract and the appendix text (patch statistics, per-repo tables) were read; the main results table was not extracted. Numbers are for 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Defines the real-world debugging test bed. Success needs localisation first, then a small edit.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Audit of SWE-agent + GPT-4 passes on SWE-bench: many passes are not real fixes. About a third had the answer in the issue or comments, and another third passed only because tests were weak.
numbers: 251 passed patches inspected: 32.67% (82) solution leakage; 31.08% suspicious due to weak tests (12.75% incorrect fixes, 14.74% changed different files or functions, 3.59% incomplete). After removing them, the resolution rate falls from 12.47% to 3.97%. On fresh post-cutoff issues (SWE-bench+) it is 0.55%. Over 94% of issues predate model cutoffs.
limits: Manual screening of passed instances only by the authors; no screening of failed ones.
agent_relevance: Test-passing is not proof. This is G3 with numbers: demand a held-out or behaviour-based check before claiming a fix.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2026) Are 'Solved Issues' in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly?
finding: PatchDiff study on SWE-bench Verified: patches from three strong tools that pass the benchmark tests often behave differently from the developer's patch, and some are plainly wrong.
numbers: 7.8% of plausible patches fail the developer-written test suite. 29.6% of plausible patches behave differently from the ground truth (46.8% from divergent implementations, 27.3% from adding extra behaviour); 28.6% of those are certainly incorrect. Reported resolution rates are inflated by 6.4 points absolute. Tools: CodeStory, LearnByInteract, OpenHands.
limits: Only three tools; manual inspection of a sample. Differential testing treats the ground-truth patch as the oracle, so some divergences may be valid alternatives.
agent_relevance: Test overfitting is measurable and common. Our S8 VERIFY should use mutated or differential checks (G3).

source: Wang et al. (2024) MINT: Evaluating LLMs in Multi-turn Interaction with Tools and Language Feedback
finding: MINT: across 20 LLMs, tools and natural-language feedback help multi-turn tasks, but RLHF and supervised instruction tuning generally hurt multi-turn skill, and single-turn strength does not predict multi-turn strength.
numbers: Gains of 1 to 8 points absolute per extra tool-use turn and 2 to 17 points from natural-language feedback (GPT-4 simulated). 91.2% of GPT-4 feedback was rated as helpful as, or better than, human feedback.
limits: Only the abstract and the feedback-quality sentence were read. Feedback comes from GPT-4, not from the model itself, so this is not self-correction.
agent_relevance: Gain comes from outside feedback, not the model's own text. Fits G2. Check our own model for multi-turn weakness before long loops (G7).
